pages.name: Push square on
pages.text: A push `F` of 150 N meets the handle square on, 0.3 m from the bolt. The arrow `r` runs from the bolt to the push. Together they span a shaded parallelogram, with area 0.3 × 150 = 45. That is the moment you already work out, the push times its distance. The [[cross product]] `r × F` is an arrow of that size, 45 N m. It stands along the bolt, because it is square to both `r` and `F`.

pages.name: Nearer the bolt
pages.task: The same 150 N push meets the handle square on, but only 0.2 m from the bolt. What is the moment's size?
pages.why: `r` runs from the bolt to the push, so it is 0.2 m long. Square on, sin 90° = 1. So the moment is 0.2 × 150 = 30 N m.

pages.name: Swing the push
pages.text: Now the push swings round toward the handle. θ is the angle between `r` and `F`. The part of `F` along the handle points straight through the bolt, so it turns nothing. Only the part square to the handle, `|F|` sin θ, turns it. So the moment's size is `|r||F|` sin θ. At 30° it halves to 22.5 N m. Along the handle it is nothing. Past the handle, the arrow flips.

pages.name: At a slant
pages.task: A 150 N push meets the handle at 30°, 0.2 m from the bolt. What is the moment's size?
pages.why: sin 30° is 0.5. So the moment is 0.2 × 150 × 0.5 = 15 N m. Only the part of the push square to the handle turns the bolt.

pages.name: Which way it points
pages.text: The [[right-hand rule]] sets the arrow's direction. Curl your right fingers from `r` toward `F`, and your thumb points along `r × F`. Turn anticlockwise, seen from above, and the arrow points out of the nut. That undoes it. Turn clockwise and the arrow points into the nut. That does it up.

pages.name: Swap the order
pages.text: Swap the order and the arrow flips, so `F × r` = −(`r × F`). The axes follow the same rule. `i × j` = `k`, but `j × i` = −`k`. Round the cycle, `j × k` = `i` and `k × i` = `j`. An arrow crossed with itself gives 0, since sin 0° = 0.

pages.task: The view has turned, so `k` points down the screen. Which way does `j × i` point?
pages.why: `i × j` = `k`, so `j × i` = −`k`, the opposite way. Here `k` points down the screen, so −`k` points up it. Turning the view changes how it looks, not the answer.

pages.name: A wire between poles
pages.text: The same rule gives the force on a wire between magnet poles. Point your fingers along the current and curl them toward the field. Your thumb gives the force. A current `I` of 10 A runs along the wire. Its length in the field, `l`, is 0.2 m. The field `B` is 0.8 T, and θ is the wire's angle to it. Lined up, the wire feels no force. Square across, it feels `IlB` sin θ = 10 × 0.2 × 0.8 × sin 90° = 1.6 N.

pages.name: Current along i
pages.task: A current of 4 A runs along `i`, through 0.25 m of wire. The field is 0.5 T along `k`. What force does the wire feel?
pages.why: The wire is square to the field, so the size is 4 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 0.5 N. For the direction, `k × i` = `j`, so `i × k` = −`j`. The force is `−0.5j` N.
